outcome.data:
[block] “It names who fixes what the check found.” “It” is unclear, and “what the check found” is awkward. Rewrite: “It says who fixes the problems the check found.”

[block] “Each one either passes the work or fails it with findings.” “Fails it” and “findings” are hard to follow. Rewrite: “Each one either approves the work or lists what needs fixing.”

[block] “When the check fails, the findings go to this agent and it runs again.” “Findings” and “agent” are unexplained. Rewrite: “When the check fails, its notes go to the person or model fixing the work, which tries again.”

[should] “The agent's job stays narrow: fix these findings, don't start over.” “Findings” is unexplained, and the sentence sounds like an instruction from inside the system. Rewrite: “The writer fixes the listed problems instead of starting over.”

[should] “Anthropic calls this evaluator-optimizer.” The page gives no support for this claim, and “evaluator-optimizer” is unexplained. Rewrite: “This pattern is also called an evaluator-optimizer.”

[block] “Some people call this an eval loop.” “Some people” is vague, and “eval” is unexplained. Rewrite: “This is also called an evaluation loop.”

[block] “Only the winner lands. The rest leave nothing behind.” “Lands” is a figure of speech, and the second sentence overclaims. Rewrite: “Only the winner is kept. The other candidates are discarded.”

[should] “Two of the three reviewers fail the first attempt.” Reviewers do not fail an attempt. Rewrite: “Two of the three reviewers reject the first attempt.”

[should] “The second attempt passes on two of three.” A person would say who agrees. Rewrite: “Two of the three reviewers approve the second attempt.”

[block] “A number sets one budget for the whole workflow. A map like `{ plan: 3, 'tests-first': 3 }` gives each target its own. Then a review that spends its budget on one agent can't starve another.” The explanation depends on unexplained terms and uses “starve” as a figure of speech. Rewrite: “A number gives the whole workflow one retry limit. A map like `{ plan: 3, 'tests-first': 3 }` gives each target its own limit. Retries used by one target do not reduce another target's limit.”

outcome.data:
- [block] “Each one either approves the work or lists what needs fixing.” A test command does neither. → “Each check either passes the work or reports what failed.”

- [block] “A test runs. When it fails, its output goes to the target, or picks which branch runs next.” The output cannot pick a branch. → “When the test fails, its output goes to the target, or its exit code picks the next branch.”

- [block] “A model from a different family reads what the writer produced and passes or fails it.” “Model family” is unexplained jargon. → “A different kind of model reads the writer’s work and either approves it or says what needs fixing.”

- [should] “Set the pass count to the number of reviewers when one dissent must be enough to send it back.” “Dissent” is stiff, and “send it back” frames feedback as rejection. → “Set the pass count to the number of reviewers when any reviewer should be able to ask for another try.”

- [should] “The writer fixes the listed problems instead of starting over.” “Writer” is unexplained here, and “listed problems” sounds formal. → “The person or model fixing the work addresses those problems instead of starting over.”

- [should] “The record keeps every round, what it found, and how many tries are left.” The list is awkward and does not say who found anything. → “The record shows every round, what the check found, and how many tries remain.”

- [should] “This pattern is also called an evaluator-optimizer.” It adds unexplained jargon without helping the reader. → “A reviewer checks the writer’s work and sends back notes for another try.”

- [should] “The offline feature team names the target and the threshold on the panel:” “Offline feature team” sounds like a product feature, not an example. → “The example team names who retries the work and how many reviewers must approve it:”

- [should] “Two of the three reviewers reject the first attempt.” “Reject” makes a feedback round sound like final failure. → “Two of the three reviewers flag problems in the first attempt.”

- [should] “Their findings go to `implement`, which runs again.” It makes an internal step name do the work of explaining the result. → “The writer gets their notes and tries again.”
